title: Local and Global Error
short: Each Euler step makes a local error of order h², and the 1/h steps together leave a global error of order h.
trouble: Students expect the error at the end to be the size of one step's error. The errors of all the steps add up, which costs one power of h.

blocks.html: In Improved Euler and Runge–Kutta Methods you met Euler's method, $y_{n+1} = y_n + hf(t_n, y_n)$, and the more accurate Heun and Runge–Kutta methods. Now we measure their error the way Truncation Error and Order of Accuracy taught: by how it shrinks with $h$. There are two different errors to keep apart.

The local error is the error of one step taken from an exact value: $y(t_n + h)$ minus the step's result when $y_n = y(t_n)$. The global error is what we actually care about: $y(T) - y_N$ at the final time, after all $N = T/h$ steps.

For a method of order $p$, the local error is $O(h^{p+1})$ and the global error is $O(h^{p})$: summing about $1/h$ local errors costs one power of $h$. Euler: local $O(h^{2})$, global $O(h)$. Heun: global $O(h^{2})$. RK4: global $O(h^{4})$.

For Euler, Taylor's theorem gives $y(t + h) = y(t) + hy'(t) + \frac{h^{2}}{2}y''(\xi)$, and the step keeps only the first two terms: local error $\frac{h^{2}}{2}y''$. Over $[0, T]$ there are $N = T/h$ steps. Each adds an error of size about $Ch^{2}$, and earlier errors are carried along (grown or damped by the equation by at most a factor $e^{LT}$, where $L$ bounds $|\partial f/\partial y|$). So the global error is at most about $N \cdot Ch^{2}\,e^{LT} = CTe^{LT}h$: order $h$.

blocks.name: slopefield

opts.task: Shrink the step $h$ and watch the Euler path approach the solution curve.

blocks.cap: Euler's method follows the slope field in straight steps. Each step misses the curve a little (local error), and the misses add up (global error).

blocks.title: One step: local error
blocks.q: For $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$, take one Euler step with $h = 0.1$. Find the local error.

blocks.title: Many steps: global error
blocks.q: Solve the same problem to $t = 1$ (exact $y(1) = e \approx 2.71828$) with $h = 0.1$ and $h = 0.05$.
steps: For $y' = y$, Euler multiplies by $1 + h$ each step: $y_N = (1 + h)^{N}$.
The global error, $0.12$, is far bigger than one local error, $0.005$: ten of them added up and grew along the way.

blocks.title: A fourth-order method
blocks.q: RK4 on the same problem gives global errors $2.08 \times 10^{-6}$ ($h = 0.1$) and $1.36 \times 10^{-7}$ ($h = 0.05$). What is the order?
steps: Order 4, and with $h = 0.1$ it is already 60,000 times more accurate than Euler, for 4 function values per step instead of 1.

blocks.name: num-error

opts.task: Compare the slopes of the three methods. Then tick "one step only" and see each slope go up by one.

blocks.cap: Global error at t = 1 against h for y′ = −2y. With "one step only", the plot shows the local error instead.

blocks.html: Expecting the error at the end to be the size of one step's error. The local errors of all $N = T/h$ steps add up (and can grow along the way), which costs one power of $h$: a method with local error $O(h^{2})$ has global error only $O(h)$. Check: halve $h$ and compare final values; for Euler the error should halve, not quarter.
